title: Code Review PR #589: Distributed Redis Session Invalidation
businessContext: PR #589 replaces in-memory JWT blacklisting with a shared Redis cluster session store to allow immediate user logout and password-reset session revocation. However, subtle race conditions and missing key TTLs expose the cluster to memory exhaustion and security bypasses.
problemStatement: Review PR #589. Detect vulnerabilities including missing TTL expiration (causing unbounded Redis RAM growth), token reuse race conditions, and improper pattern scanning with `KEYS *` (which blocks the single-threaded Redis engine in production).
constraints: Identify performance impact of `KEYS session:*` on production Redis clusters.
Identify race condition where revoked tokens can be re-issued.
Verify session key TTL alignment with JWT expiry timestamp.
candidateTasks: Flag Line 8: Missing TTL on `redis.set`. Require `EX` parameter matching token expiration to prevent Redis OOM.
Flag Line 16: `redis.keys()` blocks the Redis single thread. Replace with Redis Set indexing (`SADD user:sessions:{userId} token`) or `SCAN`.
Explain how indexing user sessions in a Set makes revocation O(1) instead of an expensive pattern search.
hints: Redis is single-threaded; commands like `KEYS *` scan the entire dictionary synchronously and lock out all other commands.
To revoke all sessions for a user efficiently, store all active session IDs in a Redis Set keyed by `user_sessions:{userId}`.
alternativeApproaches: Using a monotonic `user_token_version` column in the database/Redis: when a user logs out or resets password, increment `version = version + 1`. All tokens with older versions are immediately invalid without deleting individual keys.
commonMistakes: Suggesting `SCAN` without noting that `SCAN` is still a loop; Set-based indexing is O(1) and far superior for user-scoped lookup.
